items.stem: A 15-year-old boy has had stiff legs since early childhood. His muscles feel tight when he first stands up and starts to run, but the stiffness eases after a few minutes of continued activity. Muscles look well developed and there is no weakness. Which channel is most likely affected?
options: Skeletal muscle sodium channel only during cold exposure
items.explanation: A warm-up phenomenon, with stiffness that improves on repeated movement, and muscular hypertrophy without weakness are typical of myotonia congenita, caused by CLCN1 chloride channel dysfunction. Sodium channel disease causes paramyotonia, which worsens with repeated effort and cold. Ryanodine receptor defects underlie malignant hyperthermia and central core disease. Neuronal potassium channel antibodies cause neuromyotonia, a peripheral nerve hyperexcitability syndrome.

items.stem: A 17-year-old girl has morning jerks of both arms that make her drop her cup, and one generalized tonic-clonic seizure after a night of little sleep. EEG shows 4 to 6 Hz generalized polyspike-wave discharges. She is sexually active and wants to avoid birth defects. Which medication is the best choice?
items.explanation: Early-morning myoclonus, sleep deprivation triggers, and generalized polyspike-wave discharges define juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. Valproate is effective but carries the highest teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risk and should be avoided in people who can become pregnant. Carbamazepine and phenytoin can aggravate myoclonic and absence seizures in generalized epilepsies. Levetiracetam, or lamotrigine, treats the syndrome with a lower fetal risk.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman, 2 weeks postpartum, has a progressive headache, a left focal seizure, and mild right hand weakness. MRI shows a small left frontal hemorrhagic infarct and a filling defect in the superior sagittal sinus on venography. What is the best treatment?
options: Anticoagulation with a direct oral anticoagulant or warfarin
items.explanation: Cerebral venous thrombosis in the puerperium is treated with anticoagulation, even when a hemorrhagic venous infarct is present, because treating the thrombosis limits further injury. Initial parenteral anticoagulation is followed by warfarin or a direct oral anticoagulant, with the choice individualized after delivery. Observation alone risks extension. Antiplatelet agents are inadequate for venous thrombosis. Surgery is reserved for herniation not responding to medical care.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman treated with haloperidol for 8 years has repetitive lip smacking, tongue protrusion, and chewing movements that she cannot suppress. Antipsychotic reduction would risk relapse of her psychosis. Which treatment is most appropriate?
options: Benztropine added to the current regimen
A vesicular monoamine transporter 2 inhibitor such as valbenazine
items.explanation: Orofacial stereotyped movements after prolonged dopamine blocker exposure are tardive dyskinesia. Vesicular monoamine transporter 2 inhibitors, valbenazine or deutetrabenazine, are the evidence-based treatment, allowing continued antipsychotic therapy. Anticholinergics such as benztropine do not help and can worsen tardive dyskinesia. Raising the dose may mask movements temporarily but worsens the long-term course. Levodopa treats parkinsonism and may aggravate dyskinesia.

items.stem: A 34-year-old Black woman has several days of vomiting and intractable hiccups, followed by loss of vision in the right eye and then weakness in both legs. MRI shows a spinal cord lesion spanning five vertebral segments. Which therapy should be avoided for long-term prevention?
items.explanation: Area postrema syndrome, optic neuritis, and a longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis suggest neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, confirmed by aquaporin-4 antibody. Interferon beta, glatiramer, natalizumab, and fingolimod can worsen this disease. Effective prevention instead includes rituximab, the interleukin-6 receptor blocker satralizumab, the complement inhibitor eculizumab, and the anti-CD19 antibody inebilizumab, all of which are chosen according to access and patient factors.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man has had 3 years of progressive disinhibition, loss of empathy, compulsive eating of sweets, and apathy. His memory and visuospatial skills are relatively preserved. MRI shows frontal and anterior temporal atrophy. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Alzheimer disease with an amnestic presentation
Dementia with Lewy bodies and parkinsonism
Normal pressure hydrocephalus with gait loss
items.explanation: Early personality change, disinhibition, loss of empathy, hyperorality, and apathy with relatively spared memory and frontal and anterior temporal atrophy define behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia. Alzheimer disease usually presents with episodic memory loss. Dementia with Lewy bodies has fluctuation, visual hallucinations, and parkinsonism. Normal pressure hydrocephalus presents with gait disturbance, then cognitive slowing and urinary urgency.

items.stem: A 5-month-old boy has clusters of flexor spasms, developmental regression, and several hypopigmented macules on his trunk. Electroencephalography shows hypsarrhythmia. Which is the preferred first-line treatment for his seizures?
items.explanation: Infantile spasms with hypsarrhythmia and hypopigmented macules suggest tuberous sclerosis complex. Vigabatrin is the preferred first-line therapy for spasms caused by this disease because it is particularly effective against them. Carbamazepine and phenytoin may worsen spasms. Ethosuximide treats absence seizures and does not treat infantile spasms. Early treatment of spasms matters because delay is linked with worse developmental outcome.

items.stem: A 44-year-old man taking lithium for bipolar disorder develops vomiting and diarrhea after a viral illness. Over 2 days he has coarse tremor, slurred speech, and an unsteady gait. His serum lithium level is 2.4 mEq/L. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Isotonic saline, with hemodialysis if he worsens
Intravenous phenytoin loading for the tremor
items.explanation: Lithium is renally cleared, and volume depletion raises levels, producing coarse tremor, dysarthria, and ataxia with toxicity. Treatment is isotonic saline, stopping the drug, and hemodialysis for severe neurologic signs or high levels. Loop diuretics worsen lithium retention through volume loss. Charcoal does not bind lithium. Phenytoin does not treat the tremor and adds toxicity.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman with obesity has daily headaches worse when lying down, transient visual obscurations, and pulsatile tinnitus. Examination shows bilateral papilledema and a normal neurologic examination. MRI and venography are normal, and lumbar puncture opening pressure is 36 cm of water. What is the first-line medication?
options: Topiramate alone at a high dose
items.explanation: Positional headache, visual obscurations, pulsatile tinnitus, papilledema, normal imaging, and raised opening pressure with normal fluid composition define idiopathic intracranial hypertension. Acetazolamide plus weight loss is first-line treatment to protect vision. Topiramate has a mild carbonic anhydrase effect and can help but is second-line. Corticosteroids are not recommended. Furosemide is not an established single therapy.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man has excessive daytime sleepiness since age 17, irresistible naps that refresh him, and brief episodes of knee buckling when he laughs. A multiple sleep latency test shows a mean sleep latency of 4 minutes and sleep-onset REM periods in three naps. What is the underlying deficiency?
options: Loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra
Impaired gamma-aminobutyric acid release in the thalamus
Loss of hypocretin neurons in the lateral hypothalamus
Loss of serotonergic neurons in the raphe nuclei
items.explanation: Sleepiness, cataplexy triggered by emotion, short sleep latency, and sleep-onset REM periods define narcolepsy type 1, caused by selective loss of hypocretin-producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus, with low cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin. Loss of nigral dopamine neurons causes parkinsonism, not sleep attacks. Thalamic and raphe changes are not established mechanisms of this disorder, and the hypocretin deficit is the finding that explains both sleepiness and cataplexy.

items.stem: A 62-year-old vegan man has 6 months of paresthesias in both feet, imbalance, and slowed thinking. Examination shows loss of vibration and position sense in the legs, brisk knee jerks, and absent ankle jerks. Hemoglobin is 10.8 g/dL with macrocytosis. What is the most likely spinal cord finding on MRI?
options: Isolated anterior horn cell loss in the lumbar cord
A hyperintense lesion of the anterior spinal artery territory
Hyperintensity confined to the lateral corticospinal tracts
Dorsal column T2 hyperintensity in the cervical cord
items.explanation: Dietary deficiency, macrocytic anemia, dorsal column loss with a mixed picture of upper and lower motor neuron signs indicate subacute combined degeneration from vitamin B12 deficiency, with T2 hyperintensity in the dorsal columns. Anterior horn cell loss describes motor neuron disease. Anterior spinal artery infarction spares dorsal columns. Isolated corticospinal changes suggest primary lateral sclerosis.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man has 3 days of fever, personality change, and a focal seizure. MRI shows hyperintensity in the right medial temporal lobe. Cerebrospinal fluid has 90 lymphocytes per microliter and elevated red blood cells. What should be given immediately?
options: Intravenous acyclovir before confirmatory results return
Oral valacyclovir only after polymerase chain reaction confirmation
items.explanation: Fever, behavioral change, seizure, medial temporal imaging changes, and lymphocytic pleocytosis with red cells suggest herpes simplex encephalitis. Intravenous acyclovir should be started empirically because delay worsens outcome, and polymerase chain reaction testing confirms it. Oral treatment is insufficient for encephalitis. Ceftriaxone treats bacterial meningitis but does not cover this virus. Steroids alone would not treat the cause.

items.stem: Cervical spondylosis is known in a 68-year-old man who falls forward and strikes his chin on the pavement. He has weakness in both arms greater than both legs, burning pain in the hands, and patchy sensory loss below the neck. Which syndrome is most likely?
items.explanation: Hyperextension injury in a person with cervical spondylosis typically damages the central gray matter and medial corticospinal fibers, causing arm weakness greater than leg weakness with variable sensory loss and bladder involvement. Anterior cord syndrome causes loss of motor and pain sensation with preserved dorsal column function. Brown-Sequard is a hemisection. Posterior cord syndrome affects proprioception.

items.stem: Spinning vertigo lasting under a minute suddenly affects a 58-year-old woman whenever she rolls over in bed or looks up. There is no hearing loss. The Dix-Hallpike maneuver to the right provokes upbeating-torsional nystagmus with a latency of a few seconds that fatigues. What is the best treatment?
options: Meclizine and bed rest for a week
items.explanation: Brief positional vertigo with a latency, torsional upbeating nystagmus that fatigues, and no hearing loss is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo of the posterior canal, caused by displaced otolith debris. Canalith repositioning (the Epley maneuver) is effective and first-line. Vestibular suppressants and rest do not remove the debris and may delay compensation. Intratympanic gentamicin is for refractory Meniere disease.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man has subacute confusion and a single homogeneously enhancing periventricular mass crossing the corpus callosum on MRI. He has no immunodeficiency. What should be avoided before obtaining a biopsy if the clinical state allows?
options: Lumbar puncture even without mass effect
Corticosteroids before the tissue is obtained
Antiseizure medication at a low dose
items.explanation: A homogeneously enhancing periventricular lesion crossing the corpus callosum suggests primary central nervous system lymphoma, which is very steroid-sensitive. Steroids can cause tumor lysis and nondiagnostic tissue, so they are withheld before biopsy unless herniation threatens. Contrast imaging is necessary for evaluation. Antiseizure drugs do not impair diagnosis. Lumbar puncture is acceptable if there is no mass effect.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man wakes with a right eyelid droop and a right pupil that is dilated and fixed, with the eye turned down and out. His left arm and leg are weak, and his face on the left droops in its lower half. Where is the lesion?
items.explanation: An ipsilateral oculomotor palsy including a dilated pupil, combined with contralateral hemiparesis and lower facial weakness, is Weber syndrome, caused by a lesion in the ventral midbrain involving the exiting third nerve fascicles and the cerebral peduncle. A lateral medullary lesion causes crossed sensory loss and Horner syndrome. A cavernous sinus lesion produces multiple cranial neuropathies without hemiparesis. A capsular lesion would not cause an oculomotor palsy.

items.stem: Over two weeks, a 23-year-old woman develops psychosis, then seizures, orofacial dyskinesias, and decreased responsiveness with autonomic instability. Cerebrospinal fluid shows lymphocytic pleocytosis and antibodies to the NR1 subunit of the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor. Which investigation is most important?
options: Colonoscopy to exclude a colon tumor
items.explanation: Psychiatric onset followed by seizures, dyskinesias, decreased consciousness, and autonomic instability with antibodies to the NR1 subunit define anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis, which in young women is often associated with an ovarian teratoma. Tumor removal combined with immunotherapy improves outcomes. Testicular examination applies to men with other paraneoplastic antibodies. Bone and colon imaging are not the typical screening targets.

items.stem: A 31-year-old man with a T4 complete spinal cord injury has a sudden pounding headache, sweating above the lesion, and a blood pressure of 190/110. His heart rate is 48. What is the most appropriate first action?
options: Give a rapid intravenous fluid bolus
Start a calcium channel blocker infusion immediately
Order an urgent head CT before any intervention
Sit him upright and check bladder and clothing
items.explanation: Severe hypertension with bradycardia, headache, and flushing above the lesion in a person with an injury at T6 or above describes autonomic dysreflexia, triggered by a noxious stimulus below the lesion, most often bladder distension or fecal impaction. The first step is to sit the patient upright, loosen constrictive clothing, and find and remove the trigger, such as by catheterization. Fluids would worsen hypertension. Drugs come after removal of the trigger, and head imaging is not first.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman has double vision, unsteady walking, and absent ankle reflexes 10 days after a diarrheal illness. Examination shows bilateral partial ophthalmoplegia and limb ataxia with normal strength. Which antibody is most likely to be found?
items.explanation: The triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia after an enteric infection is Miller Fisher syndrome, a Guillain-Barre variant strongly associated with anti-GQ1b antibodies. Anti-GM1 antibodies are linked to multifocal motor neuropathy and axonal Guillain-Barre. Acetylcholine receptor antibodies cause myasthenia gravis, which spares reflexes and coordination. Anti-MAG antibodies produce a slowly progressive, sensory-predominant demyelinating neuropathy in older adults.

items.stem: A 7-year-old boy has focal seizures of the right face and hand that continue for hours each day despite three medications. Over 8 months he has developed progressive right hemiparesis and declining school performance. MRI shows progressive left hemispheric atrophy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanation: Intractable focal motor seizures with epilepsia partialis continua, progressive hemiparesis, cognitive decline, and unilateral hemispheric atrophy characterize Rasmussen encephalitis, a chronic T cell mediated inflammatory process. Sturge-Weber syndrome shows a facial capillary malformation and leptomeningeal angioma. Landau-Kleffner syndrome causes acquired aphasia with sleep-activated spikes. The hemiconvulsion syndrome follows a single prolonged febrile event, not progressive disease.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman has sudden left neck pain, a partial left Horner syndrome, and transient right arm weakness after a chiropractic neck manipulation. Which finding on vascular imaging is most likely?
options: A saccular aneurysm of the anterior communicating artery
An atherosclerotic plaque at the carotid bifurcation
Intramural hematoma with tapered narrowing of the left internal carotid artery
A fusiform dilation of the basilar artery
items.explanation: Neck pain with an ipsilateral partial Horner syndrome (miosis and ptosis without anhidrosis of the face) and ischemic symptoms indicates cervical carotid dissection, which shows a long tapered narrowing or intramural hematoma beyond the bulb. Anterior communicating aneurysms rupture into subarachnoid blood. Bifurcation plaque occurs in older patients with vascular risk. Basilar dilation presents with brainstem compression, not this syndrome.

items.stem: A 16-year-old boy has new tremor, slurred speech, and falling grades. Examination shows dystonic posturing of the hands. Slit lamp examination shows golden-brown corneal rings. Which laboratory profile is most expected?
options: High serum ceruloplasmin with low urinary copper
Low serum ferritin with high transferrin saturation
Elevated very long chain fatty acids
Low serum ceruloplasmin with elevated 24-hour urinary copper
items.explanation: Young onset movement disorder with psychiatric and hepatic features and Kayser-Fleischer rings indicates Wilson disease, an ATP7B defect of biliary copper excretion. Typical results are low ceruloplasmin, raised 24-hour urine copper, and raised hepatic copper. Ceruloplasmin is not high in this disease. Iron overload patterns suggest hemochromatosis or neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation. Very long chain fatty acids are raised in X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy.

items.stem: A 43-year-old woman with relapsing multiple sclerosis has taken natalizumab for 30 months. She is positive for anti-John Cunningham virus antibodies with a high index and has prior immunosuppressant exposure. Which statement best guides her treatment decision?
options: Her risk is removed entirely by changing to every-eight-week dosing instead
Her risk of leukoencephalopathy is high and a switch should be considered
A positive antibody result means she already has active infection of the brain
Natalizumab carries no added risk when continued beyond 24 months of use
items.explanation: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy risk with natalizumab rises with anti-John Cunningham virus antibody positivity and index, treatment beyond 24 months, and prior immunosuppression. Positive serology marks exposure, not disease. Extended-interval dosing may lower risk but does not eliminate it. Duration beyond two years clearly raises risk, so switching to another disease-modifying therapy is considered after discussion with the patient.

items.stem: A 77-year-old woman has 18 months of slowed thinking, a wide-based shuffling gait with feet that seem stuck to the floor, and urinary urgency. MRI shows enlarged ventricles out of proportion to sulcal atrophy. What is the most useful test to predict benefit from shunting?
options: A serum vitamin B12 and thyroid level
Gait testing before and after a lumbar puncture
items.explanation: Gait disturbance, cognitive slowing, and urinary urgency with disproportionate ventriculomegaly indicate normal pressure hydrocephalus. Improvement in gait after removal of 30 to 50 mL of cerebrospinal fluid, or after continuous external drainage, predicts a good shunt response. A low vitamin level is only a coexisting treatable cause. Electroencephalography does not predict benefit. Amyloid imaging would not decide shunting.

items.stem: A 14-month-old girl lost purposeful hand use after normal early development. She now wrings her hands constantly, has slowed head growth, and has episodes of breath holding and hyperventilation. Which genetic abnormality is most likely?
items.explanation: Normal early development followed by loss of hand skills, stereotyped hand wringing, deceleration of head growth, and breathing irregularities define Rett syndrome, an X-linked disorder due to MECP2 mutations, usually in girls. FMR1 expansion causes fragile X syndrome. UBE3A loss causes Angelman syndrome with happy demeanor and ataxia. SMN1 deletion causes spinal muscular atrophy, which is a motor neuron disease without these features.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman has sudden weakness of the right leg. On examination, when she is asked to flex her left hip against resistance while lying supine, her weak right leg presses downward into the examiner's hand. Reflexes and tone are normal. Which sign is demonstrated?
items.explanation: Involuntary extension of the weak leg when the contralateral leg is flexed against resistance is Hoover sign, a positive clinical sign of functional neurologic disorder. It shows that voluntary effort can be recruited automatically. A Babinski sign is an upgoing plantar response with upper motor neuron disease. Romberg sign tests proprioception. Gower sign indicates proximal weakness in muscle disease.

items.stem: A 63-year-old woman has brief electric shock pains in the right cheek and gum, triggered by chewing and a light breeze. Neurologic examination is normal. What is the most appropriate first treatment?
options: Gabapentin as a sole therapy at bedtime
items.explanation: Paroxysmal, stabbing facial pain in the trigeminal territory provoked by light touch with a normal examination is classic trigeminal neuralgia. Carbamazepine, or oxcarbazepine, is first-line and often gives a prompt response. Gabapentin is used as an adjunct. Triptans treat migraine and cluster headache. Tricyclic antidepressants help persistent neuropathic or atypical facial pain but are less effective for this disorder.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man has punched and kicked his wife during sleep several times in the past year, waking with vivid dreams of being attacked. Polysomnography confirms REM sleep without atonia. Which statement about his long-term outlook is correct?
options: He will most likely develop Huntington disease
He is at high risk of a later synucleinopathy
The disorder is benign and carries no neurologic risk
He has a high risk of developing multiple sclerosis
items.explanation: REM sleep behavior disorder with polysomnographic loss of atonia is a strong prodrome of alpha-synucleinopathies, including Parkinson disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, and multiple system atrophy, often years to decades later. Treatment includes bedroom safety and melatonin or clonazepam. Calling it benign ignores this risk. Huntington disease and multiple sclerosis are not associated with it.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman admitted with severe hyponatremia (sodium 108 mEq/L) has her level corrected to 124 mEq/L within 12 hours. Four days later she becomes quadriparetic with dysarthria, dysphagia, and impaired eye movements. Which MRI finding is most likely?
options: T2 hyperintensity in the central pons
items.explanation: A delayed neurologic decline a few days after rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia suggests osmotic demyelination, with pontine lesions causing the classic locked-in-type picture of quadriparesis and bulbar weakness. Safe correction is below 8 to 10 mEq/L in 24 hours, so the pace here was too fast. Mammillary body changes occur in Wernicke encephalopathy. Hippocampal swelling suggests limbic encephalitis.

items.stem: A 41-year-old man with advanced HIV infection has 3 weeks of headache and fever. Cerebrospinal fluid shows an opening pressure of 38 cm of water and a positive cryptococcal antigen. Which management step is most important for his symptoms?
options: Starting antiretroviral therapy on the same day
items.explanation: Cryptococcal meningitis in advanced HIV is often accompanied by raised intracranial pressure, which drives morbidity and is treated by serial lumbar punctures along with induction antifungal therapy. Corticosteroids worsen outcomes. Acetazolamide has no benefit and carries harm. Starting antiretroviral therapy early increases the risk of paradoxical immune reconstitution inflammation, so it is deferred for several weeks.

items.stem: A 71-year-old man with cervical spondylosis falls forward and hyperextends his neck. He has severe weakness and burning pain in both hands, with relatively milder leg weakness and urinary retention. Pain and temperature sensation are patchy. Which syndrome is this?
items.explanation: Hyperextension injury in an older person with a narrowed spinal canal causes central cord syndrome, with disproportionately greater arm than leg weakness, bladder dysfunction, and variable sensory loss because of the central location of cervical corticospinal fibers for the arms. Anterior cord syndrome spares dorsal column function. Brown-Sequard syndrome causes ipsilateral weakness and contralateral pain loss. Posterior cord syndrome affects proprioception and vibration.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman notices that her left pupil is larger in bright light. The pupil reacts slowly and segmentally to light but constricts more tightly with near effort and redilates slowly. Her left ankle reflex is absent. Which test would confirm the diagnosis?
options: Failure to dilate with topical cocaine drops after 1 hour
Constriction of the pupil with dilute pilocarpine
items.explanation: A large, poorly reactive pupil with light-near dissociation and a vermiform response, plus absent deep tendon reflexes, defines Adie tonic pupil. Denervation causes cholinergic supersensitivity, so a dilute pilocarpine solution constricts it while a normal pupil does not. Cocaine failure to dilate and hydroxyamphetamine response are used to localize Horner syndrome, in which the pupil is small. Apraclonidine dilates a Horner pupil through denervation supersensitivity.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman has 3 weeks of confusion and left hemiparesis. MRI shows a homogeneously enhancing periventricular mass crossing the corpus callosum. A neurosurgeon plans a biopsy. Her primary physician started dexamethasone 4 days ago with partial improvement. What should have been done?
options: Withholding corticosteroids until tissue is obtained
Resecting the lesion completely before steroids
Giving whole-brain radiation as the first step in treatment
items.explanation: A homogeneously enhancing periventricular lesion crossing the corpus callosum suggests primary CNS lymphoma, which is exquisitely corticosteroid sensitive, so steroids can shrink the mass and cause a nondiagnostic biopsy. They are withheld when possible unless herniation threatens. Definitive treatment is high-dose methotrexate-based chemotherapy after tissue diagnosis. Empiric chemotherapy or radiation without a diagnosis is inappropriate, and radical resection has no benefit in lymphoma.

items.stem: In a randomized trial of a new antithrombotic after stroke, recurrent stroke occurs in 12 percent of control patients and 8 percent of treated patients over 2 years. What is the approximate number needed to treat to prevent one recurrent stroke?
items.explanation: The absolute risk reduction is 12 percent minus 8 percent, which equals 4 percent, or 0.04. The number needed to treat is the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction, so 1 divided by 0.04 equals 25 patients over the 2 years of the trial. The relative risk reduction of one third is a different quantity, and taking its reciprocal gives the wrong figure of 3. The values 12 and 50 follow from misusing the baseline risk or halving.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man has brief, frequent, jerk-like arm and face events, up to 30 daily, along with new short-term memory loss. Sodium is 125 mEq/L. Antiseizure drugs have not helped. MRI shows medial temporal hyperintensity. Which therapy is the most appropriate?
options: Empiric antibiotic therapy for suspected bacterial meningitis
Corticosteroids with immune globulin or plasma exchange
items.explanation: Faciobrachial dystonic seizures with memory loss, hyponatremia, and medial temporal changes point to anti-LGI1 limbic encephalitis. The events respond poorly to antiseizure drugs but often stop with immunotherapy, which is also started early to prevent cognitive decline: steroids with immune globulin or plasma exchange. Further antiseizure titration alone misses the cause. The picture is not bacterial meningitis. Levodopa does not treat an immune-mediated cause.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man with diabetes loses 12 kg over 3 months and then develops severe, deep thigh pain followed by wasting and weakness of the right quadriceps. Knee reflex is absent and sensation is mildly reduced over the anterior thigh. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
options: L4 radiculopathy from a herniated disc
items.explanation: Subacute asymmetric thigh pain with proximal wasting and weight loss in a patient with diabetes defines diabetic amyotrophy, an ischemic microvasculitic radiculoplexus neuropathy that often improves slowly over time. A hematoma would follow anticoagulation or trauma and would present abruptly. A disc lesion rarely causes such widespread wasting with marked weight loss. Distal symmetric polyneuropathy begins in the feet and does not start proximally.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man is found convulsing continuously by paramedics, and 6 minutes later he is still seizing. No intravenous access can be obtained. Which first-line treatment is most appropriate?
options: Intramuscular fosphenytoin loaded at 20 mg per kg
items.explanation: Status epilepticus requires immediate benzodiazepine therapy, and when no vein is available, intramuscular midazolam is proven at least as effective as intravenous lorazepam in the prehospital setting. Fosphenytoin is a second-line agent and, although it can be given intramuscularly, it is slower and not a first-line drug. Oral drugs are unsafe during active convulsion. Propofol is reserved for refractory status in an intubated patient.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man has migraine with aura since age 25, two prior subcortical strokes, and mild apathy. His mother died of dementia after strokes. MRI shows extensive white matter hyperintensities involving the anterior temporal poles and external capsules. Which gene is most likely mutated?
items.explanation: Early migraine with aura, recurrent lacunar strokes, mood change, and anterior temporal white matter lesions with a dominant family history define CADASIL, caused by cysteine-altering NOTCH3 mutations and confirmed by genetic testing. COL4A1 mutations cause porencephaly and small vessel hemorrhage. HTRA1 causes a recessive disorder with alopecia and spondylosis. APP mutations cause early Alzheimer disease or cerebral amyloid angiopathy.

items.stem: A 69-year-old man has had slowness, a stooped posture, and repeated backward falls within 2 years. Examination shows a square-wave jerk pattern, slowed vertical saccades, and axial rigidity greater than limb rigidity, with poor response to levodopa. Which finding on brain MRI is most characteristic?
options: Hot cross bun sign in the pons
Putaminal slit-like hypointensity with a hyperintense rim
items.explanation: Early falls, vertical gaze slowing, and axial rigidity with poor levodopa response indicate progressive supranuclear palsy, a tauopathy, which shows midbrain tegmental atrophy (hummingbird sign). The hot cross bun sign is typical of multiple system atrophy with cerebellar features. Caudate atrophy is seen in Huntington disease. A slit-like putaminal rim suggests the parkinsonian type of multiple system atrophy.

items.stem: Over 4 days a 28-year-old woman notices painful dimming of vision in the left eye, worse with eye movement. Examination shows a left relative afferent pupillary defect and a normal optic disc. MRI of the brain shows three periventricular lesions. What is the best next treatment for the acute episode?
options: Oral prednisone at a low dose for 6 weeks
Observation, since recovery is not changed by treatment
items.explanation: Acute optic neuritis with periventricular lesions suggests early multiple sclerosis. High-dose intravenous methylprednisolone speeds visual recovery, though it does not change final acuity. Low-dose oral prednisone alone is associated with more recurrences of optic neuritis. Intravenous immunoglobulin has no proven benefit. Observation is acceptable only for mild deficits, and in this case treatment is reasonable because it shortens the episode.

items.stem: For 2 years a 72-year-old woman has struggled to find words and to repeat long sentences. Her speech is slow with frequent pauses, but grammar and single-word comprehension are intact. Neuroimaging shows left posterior temporal and inferior parietal atrophy. Which underlying pathology is most likely?
items.explanation: Word-finding pauses with impaired sentence repetition and preserved grammar and single-word comprehension define logopenic variant primary progressive aphasia, associated with left temporoparietal atrophy. Most patients have underlying Alzheimer disease pathology. TDP-43 type C pathology is typical of the semantic variant, and Pick bodies tend to underlie the nonfluent or behavioral variants, so neither fits this language profile.

items.stem: A 12-year-old boy has more than six cafe au lait macules, freckling in both axillae, and two cutaneous neurofibromas. Which additional finding would be expected on ophthalmologic examination?
items.explanation: Multiple cafe au lait macules, axillary freckling, and neurofibromas satisfy criteria for neurofibromatosis type 1, in which iris Lisch nodules are common and optic pathway gliomas can occur. Kayser-Fleischer rings occur in Wilson disease. A cherry-red macula is seen in lysosomal storage disorders such as Tay-Sachs disease. Retinal angiomas suggest von Hippel-Lindau disease, a separate tumor syndrome.

items.stem: A 27-year-old man started on a new antipsychotic 4 days ago has temperature of 40.1 C, severe lead-pipe rigidity, confusion, and a creatine kinase of 9,800 U/L. Deep tendon reflexes are normal. Which is the best immediate management?
options: Continue the antipsychotic and add cyproheptadine
Stop the drug and start cooling with fluids
Give an antibiotic for presumed meningitis only
Start levodopa and increase the antipsychotic
items.explanation: Fever, lead-pipe rigidity, altered mental status, and a high creatine kinase after starting a dopamine antagonist indicate neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Management starts with stopping the offending drug, cooling, and hydration, and dantrolene or bromocriptine for severe cases. Cyproheptadine treats serotonin syndrome, which shows clonus and hyperreflexia. Antimicrobials alone leave the cause untreated. Increasing a dopamine blocker would worsen the syndrome.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman has had a constant right-sided headache for 3 months, with exacerbations accompanied by ipsilateral tearing and a drooping eyelid. Triptans, nonsteroidal drugs, and a preventive migraine agent have failed. Which diagnostic test is both useful and therapeutic?
options: A trial of verapamil at 240 mg daily
High-flow oxygen at 12 L per minute
items.explanation: A continuous strictly unilateral headache with superimposed exacerbations and ipsilateral autonomic features suggests hemicrania continua, which responds absolutely to indomethacin. Verapamil is used for cluster headache prevention. Oxygen aborts cluster attacks but does not treat a continuous headache. Lamotrigine has been used in some short-lasting neuralgiform headaches, but it is not the diagnostic therapeutic standard in this presentation.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man has acted out dreams for 3 years, once punching his wife while shouting. He also has constipation and a reduced sense of smell. Polysomnography shows REM sleep without atonia. Which long-term outcome is he at greatest risk for?
options: Alzheimer disease with amyloid plaques and tangles
A synucleinopathy such as Parkinson disease
items.explanation: Dream enactment with REM sleep without atonia on polysomnography is REM sleep behavior disorder. When idiopathic, it is a strong prodromal marker, with most patients developing Parkinson disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, or multiple system atrophy over years, and constipation and hyposmia support this. It is not tied to amyloid plaque disease, demyelinating disease, or a trinucleotide repeat disorder. Bedroom safety measures and clonazepam or melatonin reduce injury.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man with a serum sodium of 106 mEq/L from a thiazide diuretic is treated with hypertonic saline. After 3 days, the sodium is 122. He then becomes dysarthric and quadriparetic with a locked-in appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Osmotic demyelination of the central pons
items.explanation: Correcting chronic hyponatremia too quickly, more than 8 mEq/L in 24 hours in high-risk patients, can cause osmotic demyelination, which appears 2 to 6 days later with dysarthria, dysphagia, spastic quadriparesis, and a locked-in state. MRI shows pontine hyperintensity. Wernicke encephalopathy presents with ophthalmoplegia and ataxia. Hepatic encephalopathy fluctuates with asterixis. A pontine hemorrhage would present abruptly and show blood on CT.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman recently diagnosed with advanced HIV (CD4 count 40) reports 2 weeks of headache and blurred vision. Opening pressure is 42 cm of water, and India ink and cryptococcal antigen are positive. Besides antifungal induction therapy, which intervention is most important?
items.explanation: Cryptococcal meningitis in advanced HIV often causes markedly raised intracranial pressure, and repeated therapeutic lumbar punctures reduce mortality and visual loss, with a goal of lowering pressure by half or to under 20 cm of water. Acetazolamide has not shown benefit and risks acidosis. Early antiretroviral therapy increases the risk of immune reconstitution syndrome and is typically delayed for several weeks. Corticosteroids increased harm in trials.

items.stem: A 17-year-old football player is struck in the head and has 10 minutes of dizziness and a headache. Examination is normal at 48 hours. His symptoms have resolved at rest. What is the recommended approach to returning to play?
options: A graded stepwise program, advancing only while symptom-free
Immediate return once the headache resolves
Strict dark-room rest for 2 weeks with no screens before activity
Return to play after a normal CT scan
items.explanation: Current guidance for concussion favors brief relative rest for 24 to 48 hours, then a stepwise return to light aerobic activity, sport-specific drills, noncontact practice, and full contact, advancing only while symptoms stay absent and stepping back if they recur. Immediate return risks a second impact. Prolonged strict rest delays recovery. A normal CT scan does not exclude concussion and does not clear an athlete.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man has sudden vertigo with vomiting for 12 hours and cannot stand. Examination shows direction-changing nystagmus on lateral gaze, a normal head impulse test, and a vertical skew deviation. What is the most likely cause?
items.explanation: Acute continuous vertigo with a normal head impulse test, direction-changing gaze-evoked nystagmus, and skew deviation is a central HINTS pattern, which is more sensitive for stroke than early MRI in the first 48 hours. Vestibular neuritis shows an abnormal head impulse, unidirectional nystagmus, and no skew. Benign positional vertigo causes brief positional episodes. Meniere disease features hearing loss and tinnitus with episodes lasting hours.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman has progressive weakness of her right hand and mild personality change. Her brother had behavioral dementia and her mother died of motor neuron disease. Genetic testing is requested. Which abnormality is the most common genetic cause of this familial syndrome?
options: CAG repeat expansion in the huntingtin gene
Point mutations in the SOD1 gene
Triplet repeat expansion in the ataxin-3 gene
items.explanation: The coexistence of motor neuron disease and frontotemporal dementia within a family points to a C9orf72 hexanucleotide expansion, the most frequent genetic cause of both familial amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia. SOD1 mutations cause a purely motor, often lower motor neuron phenotype and are second in frequency. Huntingtin repeats cause chorea and Machado-Joseph disease arises from ataxin-3 repeats.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman of Han Chinese ancestry has newly diagnosed focal epilepsy. Before starting carbamazepine, which test is recommended to lower the risk of a severe cutaneous reaction?
options: Serum drug level of the active metabolite
items.explanation: In patients of Asian ancestry, the HLA-B*1502 allele strongly predicts carbamazepine induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, so genotyping before treatment is advised and an alternative drug is chosen when positive. HLA-B*5701 testing relates to abacavir hypersensitivity. Thiopurine methyltransferase testing is relevant to azathioprine. Drug level monitoring does not predict this immune mediated reaction.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman has repeated explosive headaches reaching peak intensity within a minute, beginning two weeks after starting a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor. CT and lumbar puncture are normal, and vascular imaging shows multifocal segmental narrowing that resolves at 12 weeks. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Give triptans at the onset of each headache
Begin dual antiplatelet therapy for 3 months
Start high-dose intravenous corticosteroids for vasculitis
Stop the serotonergic agent and avoid vasoconstrictive drugs
items.explanation: Recurrent thunderclap headache with reversible multifocal arterial narrowing defines reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome, often triggered by serotonergic or vasoactive drugs. Treatment is removal of triggers, avoidance of triptans and other vasoconstrictors, and supportive care, sometimes with a calcium channel blocker. Triptans can worsen vasospasm. Antiplatelets have no role. Corticosteroids have been linked to worse outcomes and are not used.

items.stem: A 9-year-old boy has had motor and vocal tics for 3 years, with frequent shoulder jerks and throat clearing. He also has marked inattention that disrupts his schoolwork, and the tics cause him mild distress but no injury. Which medication would address both problems?
options: Methylphenidate alone at a high dose
items.explanation: Alpha-2 agonists such as guanfacine or clonidine reduce tics and also improve inattention and impulsivity, so they suit a child who has both. Stimulants are not contraindicated in tic disorders but are not expected to suppress tics. Haloperidol suppresses tics but carries extrapyramidal and metabolic burdens and is kept for severe disease. Valproate has no established role in tics.

items.stem: A 6-year-old girl develops fever, then 5 days later has drowsiness, an unsteady gait, and left optic neuritis. MRI shows large, poorly marginated white matter lesions in both hemispheres. She had an upper respiratory illness 2 weeks ago. Which is the best initial treatment?
items.explanation: A monophasic encephalopathy with multifocal deficits and large bilateral lesions after infection indicates acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, which is more common in children. First-line treatment is high-dose intravenous corticosteroids, with immunoglobulin or plasma exchange if the response is poor. Interferon beta is for established multiple sclerosis. Acyclovir treats herpes encephalitis. Cyclophosphamide is not a first-line therapy.

items.stem: A 78-year-old man with mild Alzheimer disease is started on donepezil. Two weeks later he has a brief faint while standing and an electrocardiogram shows a heart rate of 44 beats per minute. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Increase the dose gradually to improve his tolerance
Add memantine while continuing the same donepezil dose
Start an anticholinergic agent to counter nausea
Stop donepezil and evaluate for conduction disease
items.explanation: Cholinesterase inhibitors have vagotonic effects and can cause bradycardia, heart block, and syncope, especially in patients with conduction disease or those taking rate-slowing drugs. The drug should be stopped and cardiac evaluation done. Increasing the dose would worsen the effect. Memantine is a separate drug and does not treat the problem. Anticholinergics oppose the intended action of the drug.

items.stem: A 19-year-old woman has progressive gait ataxia, areflexia, and loss of vibration sense. Echocardiography shows hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and she has recently developed diabetes. Which genetic mechanism explains her condition?
options: CAG repeat expansion in the huntingtin gene
CGG repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene
GAA repeat expansion in the frataxin gene
items.explanation: Early progressive ataxia with areflexia, sensory loss, cardiomyopathy, and diabetes characterize Friedreich ataxia, an autosomal recessive disorder from a GAA repeat expansion in the first intron of the frataxin gene. A CAG expansion in the huntingtin gene causes Huntington disease. A CGG expansion in FMR1 causes fragile X tremor-ataxia syndrome in older adults. PMP22 duplication causes Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman takes lithium for bipolar disorder. She starts ibuprofen daily for knee pain. Two weeks later she has coarse tremor, vomiting, slurred speech, and gait ataxia. Her creatinine is slightly above baseline. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Idiosyncratic hepatic toxicity of the mood stabilizer
Reduced renal lithium clearance from the NSAID
Withdrawal of the antipsychotic she took previously
items.explanation: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, along with thiazide diuretics and ACE inhibitors, lower renal lithium clearance and raise serum levels, producing coarse tremor, gastrointestinal upset, dysarthria, and cerebellar signs. Lithium has a narrow therapeutic window, so the level should be checked and the drug held. Lithium is not primarily hepatotoxic. Antipsychotic withdrawal does not cause ataxia with vomiting. Serotonin toxicity features clonus, hyperreflexia, and fever.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has 2 months of a headache that is absent on waking, builds within 15 minutes of standing, and resolves when she lies flat. MRI shows diffuse pachymeningeal enhancement and downward displacement of the brainstem. What is the next best treatment if conservative measures fail?
items.explanation: A headache that is worse upright and relieved lying flat, with diffuse pachymeningeal enhancement and brain sag, defines spontaneous intracranial hypotension from a spinal CSF leak. When rest and hydration fail, an epidural blood patch is the usual treatment, with targeted patching or surgery if the leak is located. Corticosteroids are for inflammatory disease. Acetazolamide lowers CSF production and treats raised pressure. Lumbar puncture would remove more fluid and worsen the condition.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman has daytime sleepiness since adolescence, sleep paralysis, and brief episodes of knee buckling when laughing. Which findings are expected on a multiple sleep latency test?
options: Mean sleep latency over 15 minutes with no REM onsets
Mean sleep latency of 8 minutes with exclusively non-REM sleep
Mean sleep latency of 12 minutes and a single REM onset
Mean latency of 8 minutes or less and at least 2 REM onsets
items.explanation: Sleepiness with cataplexy, sleep paralysis, and a young onset describe narcolepsy type 1. The multiple sleep latency test shows a mean latency of 8 minutes or less with two or more sleep-onset REM periods; a REM onset on the preceding polysomnography may count as one. A long latency without REM periods argues against narcolepsy. A short latency with only non-REM sleep suggests sleep deprivation or idiopathic hypersomnia. One REM onset is insufficient.

items.stem: A 26-year-old man who inhales nitrous oxide canisters nightly has 3 months of tingling feet and unsteady gait. Reflexes are brisk at the knees, and vibration sense is lost at the ankles. Serum vitamin B12 is low-normal. Which laboratory test best supports the diagnosis?
options: Elevated serum copper with low ceruloplasmin
Low serum folate with normal homocysteine
Elevated serum vitamin E with low retinol
items.explanation: Nitrous oxide inactivates cobalamin, so subacute combined degeneration of the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts can occur even with a near-normal serum B12 level. Methylmalonic acid and homocysteine rise and confirm functional deficiency, and MRI may show dorsal column T2 hyperintensity. Copper deficiency produces a similar myeloneuropathy but with low copper. Folate deficiency alone is not the mechanism. Vitamin E deficiency causes ataxia with low levels, not high levels.

items.stem: A 10-week-old breastfed boy has constipation, a weak cry, poor suck, drooping eyelids, and symmetric descending weakness. Pupils react sluggishly. Reflexes are reduced. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Intravenous immune globulin for Guillain-Barre syndrome
Empiric gentamicin to clear intestinal spores
items.explanation: Descending paralysis with constipation, bulbar weakness, and sluggish pupils in an infant indicates infant botulism from intestinal colonization by Clostridium botulinum spores. Human-derived botulism immune globulin shortens illness and hospital stay and should be given early without waiting for confirmation. Equine antitoxin is reserved for older patients because of hypersensitivity risk. Standard immune globulin is not specific, and aminoglycosides worsen neuromuscular blockade.

items.stem: A 29-year-old man has had focal impaired awareness seizures with rising epigastric sensation about twice a month despite adequate trials of lamotrigine and then carbamazepine at maximum tolerated doses. MRI shows left hippocampal sclerosis. What is the best next step?
options: Adding a third antiseizure drug and waiting a year
Repeating the MRI annually without other changes
Referral to a comprehensive epilepsy center for surgical evaluation
Starting a ketogenic diet before any other step
items.explanation: Failure of two appropriately chosen and tolerated antiseizure drugs defines drug-resistant epilepsy, and the chance of seizure freedom with a third drug is low. Mesial temporal sclerosis is the most surgically remediable cause, and temporal lobectomy gives seizure freedom in a majority. Early referral reduces morbidity and risk of sudden death. Dietary therapy is a later option, and prolonged waiting is not justified.

items.stem: A 71-year-old woman presents 90 minutes after onset of right hemiparesis and aphasia. Her blood pressure is 205 over 112 mm Hg, glucose is normal, and CT shows no hemorrhage. She is otherwise eligible for thrombolysis. What is the next step?
options: Withhold thrombolysis because blood pressure is above 180 systolic
Lower blood pressure below 185 over 110 mm Hg before giving thrombolysis
Give thrombolysis now and treat blood pressure later
Order a CT angiogram first and delay all other treatment
items.explanation: Thrombolysis eligibility requires blood pressure below 185 systolic and 110 diastolic before treatment, and it must be kept below 180 over 105 for the next 24 hours. Elevated pressure is not a contraindication when it can be safely lowered with a short-acting agent such as intravenous labetalol or nicardipine. Treating after the infusion starts raises hemorrhage risk. Vessel imaging should not delay treatment.

items.stem: A man aged 74 is brought in because of day-to-day swings in alertness, vivid hallucinations of children in the room, and parkinsonism that began after the cognitive symptoms. His wife reports he acts out dreams at night. Which treatment decision is most important to avoid harm?
options: Avoid haloperidol, because he may develop severe neuroleptic sensitivity
Start olanzapine at a high dose for the hallucinations
Stop cholinesterase inhibitors to prevent worsened confusion
Give benztropine to improve cognition and tremor
items.explanation: Cognitive fluctuation, visual hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder, and parkinsonism within a year of dementia define dementia with Lewy bodies. These patients can have severe sensitivity reactions to typical antipsychotics, so they are avoided. Olanzapine also worsens motor symptoms. Cholinesterase inhibitors improve cognition and hallucinations, so stopping them would remove a useful treatment. Anticholinergics such as benztropine worsen confusion and hallucinations in this population.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis on natalizumab for 30 months reports 3 weeks of progressive clumsiness of the right hand and word-finding trouble. MRI shows a new subcortical white matter lesion without enhancement or mass effect. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Switch to interferon beta without further testing
Repeat MRI in 6 months before changing treatment
Hold natalizumab and send CSF for JC virus PCR testing
items.explanation: A new subcortical, nonenhancing lesion with subacute cognitive and motor signs in a patient on natalizumab, with risk increasing after 2 years, raises concern for progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. Therapy should be held while CSF JC virus PCR and a repeat MRI are done. High-dose steroids can worsen untreated viral infection. Switching without testing misses the diagnosis. Waiting 6 months allows irreversible damage.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man with Alzheimer disease has taken lecanemab for 3 months. He is an apolipoprotein E epsilon 4 homozygote. He now has a new headache and confusion. MRI shows sulcal effusions and parenchymal edema in the occipital lobes. What is the most likely cause?
options: Posterior circulation embolic stroke from the heart
items.explanation: Headache, confusion, and new edema with sulcal effusion shortly after starting an anti-amyloid antibody are the picture of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities with edema, which are most frequent in epsilon 4 homozygotes. Treatment is usually suspension of the drug with monitoring, because many cases resolve and some are symptomatic. Herpes encephalitis involves the temporal lobes with fever. Disease progression does not cause edema over weeks. Embolic infarcts restrict diffusion.

items.stem: A 36-year-old man has bilateral progressive hearing loss and imbalance. MRI shows bilateral vestibular schwannomas and a spinal meningioma. His mother had cataracts and a brain tumor. Which protein is deficient in this disorder?
options: Merlin, encoded by the NF2 gene on chromosome 22
items.explanation: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas with meningioma and juvenile cataracts define neurofibromatosis type 2, an autosomal dominant disorder from loss of merlin, the NF2 gene product on chromosome 22. Neurofibromin loss causes neurofibromatosis type 1, with cafe-au-lait spots and neurofibromas. Hamartin loss causes tuberous sclerosis. Loss of the VHL protein causes von Hippel-Lindau disease, with hemangioblastomas and renal tumors. Genetic testing of relatives is advised.

items.stem: A 27-year-old man with schizophrenia is mute, staring, and immobile for 3 days, holding a fixed posture and resisting passive movement. He has a temperature of 37.2 and heart rate of 96. Which immediate step is the best choice?
options: A lorazepam challenge with close monitoring
items.explanation: Mutism, posturing, negativity, and immobility define catatonia, and the first step is a lorazepam challenge, with a clear response confirming the diagnosis and guiding scheduled benzodiazepine treatment; electroconvulsive therapy is used for those who do not respond. Escalating antipsychotics can precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which should be considered if fever, rigidity, and autonomic instability develop. Haloperidol is hazardous in catatonia. Bromocriptine is reserved for malignant syndromes.

items.stem: A 41-year-old man has had 6 weeks of daily attacks of severe right orbital pain lasting 45 minutes, with tearing, nasal congestion, and agitation, always about 90 minutes after falling asleep. Which preventive therapy and pre-treatment check are most appropriate?
options: Indomethacin, with a baseline serum creatinine
items.explanation: Strictly unilateral orbital pain with autonomic features, restlessness, and a circadian pattern describe cluster headache. Verapamil is the first-line preventive, and it can cause PR prolongation and heart block at higher doses, so an electrocardiogram is obtained before and during dose escalation. Beta blockers are used for migraine. Topiramate is a second-line option. Indomethacin is the diagnostic treatment for paroxysmal hemicrania and hemicrania continua.

items.stem: A 4-month-old girl has been floppy since birth with bell-shaped chest, tongue fasciculations, and absent deep tendon reflexes, yet she is alert and socially engaged. Genetic testing confirms homozygous SMN1 deletion. Which finding best predicts the severity of her disease?
options: The number of SMN2 gene copies
The size of the SMN1 deletion
items.explanation: Spinal muscular atrophy results from loss of SMN1, and the neighboring SMN2 gene produces a small amount of functional protein. Fewer SMN2 copies predict earlier onset and a more severe phenotype, and the count also guides treatment decisions such as disease modifying therapy. The creatine kinase level is normal or mildly raised and does not predict severity. Deletion size and fasciculation timing carry little prognostic value.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman describes episodes of a rising epigastric sensation and a feeling of familiarity, followed by lip smacking and unresponsiveness for 90 seconds. She had a prolonged febrile seizure at age 2. Which MRI finding is most likely?
options: A cortical tuber with radial white matter bands
A periventricular nodular heterotopia lining the ventricle
Unilateral hippocampal atrophy with increased T2 signal
A small cavernous malformation in the frontal lobe
items.explanation: Rising epigastric sensation, deja vu, and automatisms with impaired awareness point to mesial temporal onset, and a childhood prolonged febrile seizure is a classic antecedent of hippocampal sclerosis. MRI shows hippocampal volume loss with T2 and FLAIR hyperintensity. Tubers belong to tuberous sclerosis, which more often presents with infantile spasms. Heterotopia and cavernous malformations can cause epilepsy but do not fit this semiology and history.

items.stem: A 36-year-old man develops right-sided neck pain and a headache after a vigorous coughing spell. The next day he has a drooping right eyelid with a small right pupil, intact sweating of the forehead, and transient left hand clumsiness. Which test is most appropriate next?
options: CT or MR angiography of the head and neck
Carotid duplex ultrasound repeated in 3 months
items.explanation: Neck pain, a partial Horner syndrome with preserved forehead sweating (postganglionic involvement), and transient hemispheric symptoms are typical for cervical internal carotid dissection, which can follow minor trauma such as coughing. Cross-sectional angiography of the head and neck shows the tapered narrowing or intramural hematoma. A bubble study looks for right-to-left shunting. Lumbar puncture is for suspected hemorrhage or pressure disorders. Delaying imaging risks an avoidable stroke.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man has slurred speech, a coarse wing-beating tremor of the arms, and new depression over 8 months. Slit-lamp examination shows golden-brown rings at the corneal limbus. Which result is most likely?
options: Low 24-hour urinary copper with elevated hepatic iron
Raised 24-hour urinary copper with low ceruloplasmin
Elevated serum ferritin with normal ceruloplasmin
items.explanation: Young-onset tremor, dysarthria, psychiatric change, and Kayser-Fleischer rings indicate Wilson disease, an ATP7B defect causing copper accumulation. Typical findings are low ceruloplasmin, increased 24-hour urinary copper, and elevated hepatic copper on biopsy. Raised serum copper and ceruloplasmin would be unusual. Low urinary copper and hepatic iron overload suggests hemochromatosis. A raised ferritin with normal ceruloplasmin does not explain the corneal rings or the movement disorder.

items.stem: A 9-year-old boy has bilateral visual loss with marked optic disc swelling over 4 days, following a viral illness. Visual acuity is 20/200 in both eyes with pain on movement. MRI shows long, anterior optic nerve enhancement and no brain lesions. Which antibody is most likely positive?
options: Aquaporin-4 IgG with positive oligoclonal bands
items.explanation: Bilateral optic neuritis with prominent disc swelling and long anterior optic nerve involvement in a child is typical of myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody disease. It responds well to high-dose corticosteroids but often relapses, so antibody status guides follow-up. Aquaporin-4 antibody causes neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, which more often affects the chiasm and posterior nerve with worse recovery. NMDA receptor and GAD65 antibodies cause encephalitis and stiff-person spectrum disorders.

items.stem: A 63-year-old teacher has had 3 years of increasing trouble finding words. She can no longer name common objects such as a key, and asks 'what is a key?' when it is mentioned. Speech is fluent and grammar is intact, and her day-to-day memory is good. Where is atrophy most likely found?
options: The dominant posterior inferior frontal gyrus
The anterior temporal lobes, left more than right
The bilateral medial parietal cortex and precuneus regions
The occipital lobes with preserved temporal lobes
items.explanation: Fluent speech with loss of word meaning, impaired object naming and comprehension, and preserved grammar and episodic memory describes the semantic variant of primary progressive aphasia. It is associated with anterior temporal atrophy, usually worse on the left. The nonfluent variant involves the left inferior frontal region and produces effortful, agrammatic speech. Medial parietal atrophy fits logopenic or Alzheimer disease. Occipital atrophy suggests posterior cortical atrophy.

items.stem: A 14-month-old girl lost purposeful hand use and previously acquired words. She has constant midline hand wringing, breath holding, and a deceleration of head growth. Which gene is most likely mutated?
items.explanation: Regression after a period of normal development, with loss of hand skills, stereotyped hand wringing, and slowing of head growth in a girl, describes Rett syndrome, caused by MECP2 mutations that arise de novo in most cases. UBE3A abnormalities cause Angelman syndrome. FMR1 expansion causes fragile X syndrome. SMN1 deletion causes spinal muscular atrophy, which presents with weakness rather than regression.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man with Parkinson disease has well-formed visual hallucinations of children and a poor tolerance of dopamine blockade. His levodopa dose has already been reduced. Which medication is the best choice for his psychosis?
items.explanation: Parkinson disease psychosis is treated after simplifying dopaminergic therapy. Pimavanserin, a selective serotonin 5-HT2A inverse agonist without dopamine receptor blockade, is approved for this use, and quetiapine or clozapine are other options. Haloperidol, risperidone, and olanzapine block dopamine D2 receptors strongly and can markedly worsen parkinsonism, so they should be avoided, and clozapine needs blood count monitoring if chosen.

items.stem: A 67-year-old woman has had 4 months of difficulty climbing stairs and combing her hair. She stopped atorvastatin 3 months ago, but weakness has kept worsening. Creatine kinase is 6,200 U/L, and biopsy shows necrotic fibers with little lymphocytic infiltrate. Which finding is most likely to be positive?
options: Antibodies against histidyl-tRNA synthetase with anti-Ro52 markers
Antibodies against the nuclear helicase Mi-2
items.explanation: Progressive proximal weakness that continues after statin withdrawal, with a very high creatine kinase and necrosis without much inflammation, indicates immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy with anti-HMGCR antibodies, which needs immunotherapy. Anti-Jo-1 marks antisynthetase syndrome with interstitial lung disease and arthritis. Anti-Mi-2 is tied to classic dermatomyositis with skin findings. Anti-cN1A is associated with inclusion body myositis, which causes finger flexor and quadriceps weakness.

items.stem: A 22-year-old woman reports early morning jerks of both arms that make her drop her coffee cup, and one generalized convulsion after a night of little sleep. EEG shows 4 to 6 hertz generalized polyspike and wave. She plans to become pregnant within a year. Which medication is the most appropriate choice?
items.explanation: Morning myoclonic jerks, sleep-deprivation seizures, and generalized polyspike discharges describe juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. Valproate is highly effective but carries the highest teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risk, so it is avoided in women who may conceive. Carbamazepine and phenytoin are sodium channel blockers that can aggravate myoclonic and absence seizures. Levetiracetam is effective across generalized types and has a lower fetal risk, making it a preferred option.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman, 10 days postpartum, has a worsening diffuse headache and then a focal seizure involving the left arm. Examination shows mild papilledema. Noncontrast head CT shows a small right parietal hemorrhage. Which study is most likely to reveal the cause?
options: Conventional digital subtraction angiography of the carotid arteries only
items.explanation: Postpartum status is a hypercoagulable state, and headache with papilledema, seizure, and a cortical hemorrhage not following an arterial territory strongly suggest cerebral venous thrombosis. Magnetic resonance venography or CT venography confirms a filling defect in a venous sinus or cortical vein. Arterial angiography alone may miss the venous phase. Echocardiography looks for cardioembolic sources, and electroencephalography characterizes seizures but does not identify the lesion.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man has had 2 years of unexplained backward falls, a stiff axial posture, slowed vertical saccades, and a staring facial expression. He has had a poor response to levodopa. Which MRI finding is most characteristic?
options: Hot cross bun sign in the pons
Putaminal rim hyperintensity with slit-like atrophy
Midbrain atrophy with the hummingbird sign
items.explanation: Early postural instability with falls, vertical gaze slowing, axial rigidity, and poor levodopa response define progressive supranuclear palsy. Midbrain atrophy on sagittal MRI produces the hummingbird sign. The hot cross bun sign and putaminal rim change are described in multiple system atrophy, which features dysautonomia and cerebellar or parkinsonian signs. Prominent hippocampal atrophy characterizes Alzheimer disease, not this movement syndrome.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman has 4 days of intractable hiccups and nausea, followed by a longitudinally extensive cervical cord lesion on MRI. Aquaporin-4 antibody is positive. Which disease-modifying drug used in multiple sclerosis should be avoided in her?
items.explanation: Intractable hiccups and vomiting indicate area postrema syndrome, and with a longitudinally extensive myelitis and aquaporin-4 antibodies this is neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder. Interferon beta, along with natalizumab and fingolimod, can worsen the disease and should be avoided. Satralizumab, which blocks the interleukin-6 receptor, inebilizumab, which depletes CD19 cells, and rituximab, which depletes CD20 cells, are accepted preventive therapies.

items.stem: An 82-year-old woman has had falls and urinary urgency for a year, followed by mild forgetfulness. Her gait is wide-based and magnetic. MRI shows enlarged ventricles out of proportion to sulcal atrophy. Which result best predicts a good response to shunting?
options: Gait improvement after a high-volume lumbar puncture
A markedly elevated opening pressure above 30 cm of water
items.explanation: Gait disturbance first, then urinary urgency and cognitive slowing, with ventriculomegaly out of proportion to atrophy, defines normal pressure hydrocephalus. Gait improvement after removing 30 to 50 mL of CSF, or after extended drainage, is the best bedside predictor of shunt benefit. Opening pressure is normal in this disease. Gait symptoms are the most responsive feature, not their absence. Asymmetric parietal atrophy suggests a neurodegenerative process that would not respond.

items.stem: A 3-year-old boy has absent speech, an ataxic gait with arms held up, frequent unprovoked laughter, and generalized seizures. He has fair hair for his family and a wide mouth. Which mechanism most commonly underlies his disorder?
options: Deletion of the paternally inherited chromosome 15q11 to q13 region
Deletion of the maternally inherited chromosome 15q11 to q13 region
Trinucleotide CGG expansion in a gene on the long arm of the X chromosome
Duplication of a segment of the short arm of chromosome 17
items.explanation: Absent speech, ataxia, happy demeanor with frequent laughter, and seizures describe Angelman syndrome. The most common cause is a deletion of the maternal 15q11 to q13 region, which removes the UBE3A gene, because only the maternal copy is active in neurons. The same region deleted on the paternal chromosome causes Prader-Willi syndrome, with hypotonia and hyperphagia. CGG expansion in FMR1 causes fragile X syndrome. 17p duplication causes a different disorder.

items.stem: A 19-year-old college rower develops a foot drop after sitting cross-legged for several hours. Two years ago he had a transient wrist drop after leaning on his elbow. His father had similar episodes. Nerve conduction studies show diffusely prolonged distal motor latencies. Which genetic abnormality is most likely?
options: Heterozygous deletion of the PMP22 gene on chromosome 17
Duplication of the PMP22 gene on chromosome 17
Point mutation in the GJB1 gene on the X chromosome
Point mutation in the MFN2 gene on chromosome 1
items.explanation: Recurrent painless pressure palsies in a young person with a dominant family history and diffuse slowing indicate hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies, caused by PMP22 deletion. PMP22 duplication causes Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 1A, a progressive length-dependent demyelinating neuropathy without recurrent focal palsies. GJB1 mutations cause X-linked Charcot-Marie-Tooth with intermediate velocities. MFN2 mutations cause an axonal form with normal or near-normal velocities.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man is found seizing at a bus stop. Paramedics find no intravenous access, and generalized tonic-clonic movements have lasted 8 minutes. His weight is estimated at 80 kg. Which initial treatment is best supported by trial evidence in this setting?
options: Oral clobazam 20 mg dissolved in water
Intravenous levetiracetam through an intraosseous line only after 20 minutes
items.explanation: Status epilepticus needs a benzodiazepine within minutes. When intravenous access is not available, intramuscular midazolam at 10 mg for patients over 40 kg was shown to be at least as effective as intravenous lorazepam in the prehospital setting. Oral clobazam is not appropriate in an actively convulsing patient. Phenytoin is a second-line agent that cannot be given intramuscularly because of erratic absorption. Delaying treatment for 20 minutes worsens outcomes.

items.stem: A 79-year-old man taking apixaban for atrial fibrillation arrives 90 minutes after sudden right arm weakness and drowsiness. CT shows a 40 mL left basal ganglia hemorrhage. His last apixaban dose was 5 hours ago. Which reversal agent is the most appropriate?
items.explanation: Direct factor Xa inhibitor related intracerebral hemorrhage should be reversed quickly, and andexanet alfa is the specific agent that binds the inhibitor; prothrombin complex concentrate is an accepted alternative when it is unavailable. Vitamin K reverses warfarin, not apixaban. Fresh frozen plasma gives too little factor for rapid correction and risks volume overload. Desmopressin has a role in platelet dysfunction, such as from antiplatelet drugs, and is not a reversal agent here.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman has taken haloperidol for 11 years for schizoaffective disorder. She now has repetitive lip smacking and tongue protrusion that embarrass her. Her psychiatrist wants to continue antipsychotic treatment. Which medication most directly targets her movements?
options: Amantadine started at a high dose with no taper
items.explanation: Repetitive orofacial movements after prolonged dopamine-blocker exposure describe tardive dyskinesia. Vesicular monoamine transporter 2 inhibitors such as valbenazine and deutetrabenazine are first-line, depleting presynaptic dopamine, and require monitoring for depression and parkinsonism. Anticholinergics such as benztropine can worsen tardive dyskinesia. Propranolol helps akathisia and tremor rather than orofacial dyskinesia. Amantadine has limited evidence and is not first-line.

items.stem: A 6-year-old girl develops fever, headache, and drowsiness 2 weeks after an upper respiratory infection, then ataxia and a left hemiparesis. MRI shows multiple large, poorly demarcated white matter lesions. CSF has a mild lymphocytic pleocytosis. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
items.explanation: Encephalopathy and multifocal deficits after a viral illness, with large bilateral white matter lesions on MRI, indicate acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, which is usually monophasic. First-line treatment is high-dose intravenous corticosteroids, with immunoglobulin or plasma exchange for poor responders. Acyclovir is for herpes encephalitis, which tends to involve the temporal lobes. Cyclophosphamide is far too aggressive for a self-limited disorder. Observation risks permanent deficits.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man develops personality change, hyperorality, compulsive eating of sweets, and loss of empathy over 3 years. Memory and visuospatial testing are normal. His brother has a similar illness. Which gene is most commonly responsible in familial forms?
items.explanation: Disinhibition, hyperorality, and loss of empathy with spared memory describe behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia. The most common genetic causes of familial disease are C9orf72 repeat expansions, then MAPT and GRN mutations. C9orf72 expansions also cause motor neuron disease. Presenilin 1 and amyloid precursor protein variants cause early-onset Alzheimer disease. Huntington disease produces chorea with cognitive decline.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman with dry eyes and dry mouth reports 6 months of numbness beginning in her fingers and face, then spreading to the trunk and legs, with a clumsy, unsteady gait. Reflexes are absent and strength is normal. Nerve conduction studies show absent sensory responses with normal motor studies. Where is the primary site of pathology?
options: Anterior horn cells of the spinal cord
items.explanation: A non-length-dependent sensory loss that starts in the face and arms, with sensory ataxia, absent reflexes, and widespread loss of sensory potentials, is a sensory neuronopathy. The neurons of the dorsal root ganglia are destroyed, a pattern linked to Sjogren syndrome and paraneoplastic disease. Anterior horn disease is motor and spares sensation. Small fiber disease produces pain and autonomic signs with preserved sensory potentials. Junction disorders cause fatigable weakness.

items.stem: A 28-year-old man of Han Chinese ancestry is diagnosed with focal epilepsy. His physician plans to start carbamazepine. Which preparatory step most reduces the risk of a severe cutaneous reaction?
options: Testing for HLA-B*1502 genotype before the first dose
Checking a baseline serum sodium and repeating it weekly
Titrating the dose over 6 months without testing
items.explanation: Carbamazepine and the related oxcarbazepine carry a strong association between HLA-B*1502 and Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis in patients of Southeast Asian ancestry, so genotyping is recommended before starting. Sodium monitoring addresses hyponatremia, a different adverse effect. An electrocardiogram is relevant to drugs affecting cardiac conduction. Slow titration reduces rash from lamotrigine but does not remove the genetic risk with carbamazepine.

items.stem: A 71-year-old woman had a transient episode of left monocular vision loss 6 days ago. Duplex and CT angiography show a 78 percent stenosis of the left internal carotid artery by NASCET criteria. She is otherwise well, with a life expectancy over 5 years. What is the best management?
options: Observation with dual antiplatelet therapy for 1 year
Carotid endarterectomy within 2 weeks of the ischemic event
Carotid endarterectomy after 6 months of medical therapy
Intracranial stenting of the left middle cerebral artery
items.explanation: Symptomatic carotid stenosis of 70 to 99 percent has a large absolute benefit from revascularization, and the benefit is greatest when surgery is done within 2 weeks of the event. Medical therapy alone leaves a high early recurrence risk. Waiting 6 months forfeits the early-risk benefit, which is concentrated in the first weeks. Intracranial stenting addresses a different lesion and is not recommended for this extracranial disease.

items.stem: A 14-year-old boy has progressive rigidity, drooling, school decline, and generalized seizures. His father developed chorea in his late 20s and is now institutionalized. Which genetic concept best explains the early onset in the boy?
options: Heteroplasmy shifts in maternally transmitted mitochondrial DNA
Expansion of the CAG repeat during paternal transmission
Contraction of a GAA repeat during transmission
items.explanation: Rigidity, seizures, and cognitive decline in a teenager with an affected father describe juvenile Huntington disease, the Westphal variant. The CAG repeat in HTT is especially unstable in spermatogenesis, so paternal transmission yields larger expansions and earlier onset, an example of anticipation. Imprinting at chromosome 15 underlies Angelman and Prader-Willi syndromes. Mitochondrial heteroplasmy is maternally inherited. GAA repeat expansion causes Friedreich ataxia.

items.stem: A 48-year-old man has had steadily worsening spastic leg weakness over 2 years, without relapses. MRI shows spinal cord and periventricular lesions, and CSF has oligoclonal bands. Which treatment is approved for this disease course?
