items.explanation: A steady progression of disability from onset, without relapses, with typical lesions and oligoclonal bands, describes primary progressive multiple sclerosis. Ocrelizumab, a CD20-depleting antibody, is the first therapy shown to slow disability progression in this form, and it is also used in relapsing disease, so a patient needs no prior relapses to qualify. The other agents are approved for relapsing forms and have not shown benefit in primary progressive disease.

items.stem: A 38-year-old man has had slowly progressive difficulty rising from the floor and recent morning headaches with daytime sleepiness. Examination shows mild proximal weakness and a weak neck flexion. Creatine kinase is mildly elevated, and forced vital capacity falls 25 percent when supine. Which test best establishes the diagnosis?
options: Acid alpha-glucosidase enzyme activity in blood
Dystrophin gene deletion and duplication analysis
Repetitive stimulation at 3 hertz of the ulnar nerve
items.explanation: Limb-girdle pattern weakness with early diaphragm involvement, shown by the supine drop in vital capacity, suggests late-onset Pompe disease. Measuring acid alpha-glucosidase activity, often on a dried blood spot, confirms it, and enzyme replacement therapy is available. Dystrophin testing addresses Duchenne and Becker dystrophy, which rarely start with respiratory failure in adulthood. Repetitive stimulation evaluates junction disease. Forearm exercise testing is for glycogenolysis defects such as McArdle disease.

items.stem: A 5-month-old girl with several hypopigmented macules on the trunk has clusters of brief flexor spasms on awakening. EEG shows a chaotic high-voltage background with multifocal spikes. Echocardiography shows a cardiac rhabdomyoma. Which treatment is the best first choice for the spasms?
items.explanation: Infantile spasms with hypsarrhythmia in a child with hypopigmented macules and a cardiac rhabdomyoma indicate tuberous sclerosis complex. Vigabatrin is the preferred first-line therapy for spasms in this disorder because it targets GABA transaminase and has a high response rate, with periodic vision monitoring for retinal toxicity. Carbamazepine can worsen spasms. Phenobarbital and lamotrigine have little efficacy for this syndrome.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman is recovering from an aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage treated with coiling 6 days ago. Her serum sodium has fallen to 126 mEq/L. She is hypovolemic, with urine sodium of 60 mEq/L and high urine output. Which treatment is most appropriate?
options: Strict fluid restriction to 1 liter daily
items.explanation: Hyponatremia with hypovolemia and high urinary sodium after subarachnoid hemorrhage reflects cerebral salt wasting, which needs volume and sodium replacement, with fludrocortisone as an adjunct. Fluid restriction is the treatment for the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis in euvolemic patients and would worsen hypovolemia, raising the risk of delayed cerebral ischemia from vasospasm. Furosemide with free water worsens sodium and volume loss. Demeclocycline is a slow treatment for chronic inappropriate antidiuresis.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman with Parkinson disease started pramipexole 3 years ago. Her restless legs symptoms now begin at 2 PM instead of at night, spread to her arms, and are more severe. Her serum ferritin is 90 ng/mL. What is the best management?
options: Increase the dopamine agonist dose by 50 percent
Add a second dopamine agonist at bedtime and continue the first
Taper the agonist and start gabapentin enacarbil
Switch to a daily low-dose opioid at bedtime
items.explanation: Earlier daily onset, spread to the arms, and greater severity after long dopaminergic treatment define augmentation of restless legs syndrome. Raising the agonist dose worsens augmentation over time. Adding a second agonist does the same. Guidelines favor alpha-2-delta ligands such as gabapentin enacarbil, gabapentin, or pregabalin as first-line therapy, and the offending agonist is tapered. Iron is given when ferritin is 75 or lower, and opioids are reserved for refractory cases.

items.stem: A 29-year-old man of Thai descent awakens with flaccid weakness of both legs after a large pizza dinner the evening before. He has weight loss, tremor, and a resting pulse of 118. Serum potassium is 2.1 mEq/L. In addition to cautious potassium replacement, which treatment prevents recurrence?
options: Treatment of hyperthyroidism and a nonselective beta blocker
Lifelong daily acetazolamide without addressing thyroid status
Calcium gluconate infusion with a high-potassium diet
items.explanation: Episodic weakness after a carbohydrate load, with hypokalemia and clinical thyrotoxicosis, defines thyrotoxic periodic paralysis, most often in men of Asian ancestry. Attacks stop when euthyroidism is restored, and propranolol blunts the adrenergic drive that shifts potassium into cells. Acetazolamide can worsen some forms and does not treat the cause. Calcium helps hyperkalemic episodes. Immunotherapy is for inflammatory neuropathy, which does not cause reversible hypokalemic attacks.
